item.title: Conservative Consumer Movements and Reactionary Forms of Consumption
item.content:encoded:
Alisa Minina Jeunemaitre, emlyon business school

Stefania Masè, IPAG Business School

This special issue examines how conservative, populist, and reactionary consumer movements use consumption as a cultural and political practice. While progressive consumer movements have received substantial scholarly attention, conservative consumer movements remain understudied and often analyzed through frameworks of extremism or social danger. The editors seek contributions that adopt an emic approach, understanding these movements from participants' perspectives while maintaining critical analysis.

The issue welcomes interdisciplinary research exploring how conservative consumer practices construct political, religious, gendered, and national identities. Contributors are encouraged to distinguish analytically among conservatism, populism, reactionary politics, and related categories rather than treating them as interchangeable. Research should examine how markets, brands, platforms, and material practices shape these movements, what needs they express, what forms of belonging they create, and whether consumption can facilitate dialogue across ideological differences.

Appel publié par Consumption Markets & Culture. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Tradwife and gendered lifestyle movements
  • Conservative and populist consumer activism
  • Religious consumption and faith-based markets
  • Religious influencers and religious marketing
  • Prepper, survivalist, and self-sufficiency movements
  • Conspiracy theories and consumer communities
  • Gun cultures and influencer economies
  • Nationalist and anti-globalist consumption
  • Modest fashion
  • Anti-multicultural and antiprogressive market practices
  • Boycotts, buycotts, and ideological consumption
  • Platforms and circulation of political identities
  • Consumer culture and family values
  • Traditionalism, nostalgia, and heritage
  • Domesticity and conservative subject formation
  • Market responses to reactionary and populist movements
  • Consumption and dialogue across ideological divisions

Timeline

  • February 28, 2027: Manuscript submission deadline

item.title: Populism and Public Management
item.content:encoded:
Zoe Radnor, Aston University

David Walker, Oxford Health NHS Foundation Trust

This special issue examines the intersection of populism and public management, inviting cross-disciplinary perspectives from law, social sciences, politics and public administration. The rise of populist movements worldwide, spanning both left and right of the political spectrum, raises fundamental questions about how public managers and administrators navigate their responsibilities when faced with politicians whose values may conflict with liberal democratic principles and established governance standards.

The issue seeks contributions that explore critical tensions in public administration under populism: whether public managers have ethical obligations to defend democratic institutions, how they balance political responsiveness with professional integrity, and whether existing accountability frameworks adequately address challenges posed by populist policies. Contributors are encouraged to consider international comparisons and examine how different governmental structures and civil service frameworks respond to populist pressures.

Appel publié par Public Money & Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Are we facing the limits of traditional thinking in public management? Do public managers have a 'moral personality' with value commitment to liberal democracy and/or state continuity?
  • Does populism create a challenge for public managers to abide by good governance principles?
  • Are public managers obliged to defend the state from attack, rhetorical or actual?
  • Have public managers traditionally lacked 'voice' within the political–administrative interface and what challenges do they face with the rise of populism?
  • Is there a problem facing public managers if they are becoming answerable to politicians with antagonistic value sets or who may break the law?
  • How anachronistic are Weberian doctrines of 'responsiveness' in the face of populism?
  • What is 'extremism'/populism and can it be defined ex ante?
  • Do public managers observe/answer to a code that protects them against orders?
  • How far do existing doctrines of accountability accommodate answerability for extremist policies?
  • Do public managers have ethical commitments that equip them to resist political directives that might subvert constitutional order?
  • What lessons could public managers learn from international and comparative perspectives on populism?
  • Is the UK a special case with its uncodified constitutional system?

Timeline

  • January 31, 2027: Submission deadline for research articles and new development pieces
  • March 31, 2027: Submission deadline for debate pieces
